questions.q: How does this lesson frame a legacy system, rather than as an embarrassing mistake?
options: As a constraint the current architecture has to design around, similar to a building's load-bearing wall during a renovation
As proof that the original architects were incompetent
As a system that should always be replaced immediately regardless of cost
As a system with no legitimate reason to still be in use
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly reframes legacy systems as a constraint to design around rather than a mistake to shame -- a current architecture has to work within that reality, the way a renovation has to work around a load-bearing wall.

questions.q: What is the strangler-fig pattern, as described in this lesson?
options: Immediately shutting down a legacy system and replacing it all at once over a single weekend

Gradually building new functionality around a legacy system's edges, routing more responsibility to new components over time, and decommissioning the legacy system only once nothing is left for it to do
A pattern for encrypting legacy system data at rest
A method for assigning classification labels to legacy data
questions.explain: The strangler-fig pattern, named after the vine that gradually grows around and eventually replaces a host tree, applies the same idea to systems: build around the legacy system's edges, shift responsibility gradually, and decommission only once it has nothing left to do.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what should an architect do if a legacy system can only produce a nightly batch file?
options: Specify a real-time integration design anyway and hope the legacy system's owners will somehow make it work
Accept that limitation in the design, rather than specifying a real-time flow the legacy system can't actually support
Refuse to integrate with the legacy system at all under any circumstances
Assume the limitation will resolve itself once Salesforce is implemented
questions.explain: The lesson insists on designing honestly around real constraints -- if a legacy system can only produce a nightly batch, the integration design has to accept that limitation rather than specifying a real-time flow that the system genuinely cannot support.

questions.q: How does this lesson define technical debt at the enterprise level?
options: A term that only applies to poorly written source code, never to systems or integrations
The accumulated cost of past shortcuts -- such as an undocumented legacy integration or an unaddressed workaround -- that creates ongoing maintenance burden or constrains future options
The literal financial debt a company owes for its software licenses
A one-time cost paid off completely the moment a new system is launched
questions.explain: At the enterprise level, the lesson extends technical debt beyond code to include things like an undocumented legacy integration or an old unaddressed workaround -- accumulated costs that constrain future options, not a one-time, code-only concept.

questions.q: What does this lesson say happens to technical debt over time if it's built around rather than addressed?
options: It automatically resolves itself as new systems are added
It compounds -- each new system built around an existing piece of debt without addressing it makes the eventual cost of addressing it later higher, not lower
It has no effect on the cost of future changes
It only affects the original system and never spreads to anything built around it
questions.explain: The lesson compares technical debt to financial debt: it compounds, and each new system built around existing debt without resolving it raises, rather than lowers, the eventual cost of eventually addressing it.
